verdict.outcome_rationale: This is a genuine agent-fault failure and the verifier's FAIL is correct. The GSO verifier compared the agent patch against baseline and reference commit bfaf917 ("PERF: Avoid np.divmod in maybe_sequence_to_range") across 20 held-out workloads, reported opt_commit=False with continuous reward 0.483, and applied a pass threshold of 1.2 that the patch did not meet [1][2][3][4]. The task asked to optimize pd.core.indexes.base.maybe_sequence_to_range while preserving outputs [5], and the known reference fix replaces the expensive np.divmod path with a Cython is_sequence_range check [4]. The agent instead iterated on pure-Python early exits—ndarray fast path, cached scalars, and adjacent-difference rejection—but left np.divmod in the hot path [6][7]. That helped the instruction's random-million-element benchmark (test 0 dropped to ~0.000015s) yet left arithmetic-range workloads far slower than the reference commit, e.g. test 1 at ~0.0075s versus ~0.00057s on the commit [8][9]. The agent declared success after local timing on only the random-input scenario (~1e-6s median) and 195 self-generated equivalence cases, without measuring performance on range-convertible inputs where divmod dominates [10]. Correctness was preserved (all eqchecks passed), but for this continuous-reward GSO task that is insufficient: the patch is roughly half the speed of the reference commit overall and does not meet the required threshold, so it was not truly solved [1][2][8].

evidence.claim: The pre-patch baseline still allocates and calls np.divmod over the full sequence for range detection.
The agent's final patch kept np.divmod and added early-exit heuristics plus an ndarray fast path rather than eliminating divmod.

On test 0 (random integers matching the instruction benchmark) the agent patch was very fast (~0.000015s), but on test 1 (million-element arithmetic arange) it remained ~0.0075s while the reference commit ran ~0.00057s.
